headline: The quote you already gave is your cheapest lead
points: Day 14: keep it open, or close it?
x:
Most quotes that go quiet aren't a no. People got busy.

Day 2: "Did it come through okay?"
Day 7: answer the price or timing worry.
Day 14: "Keep it open, or close it out?"

How many follow-ups does your shop send now?
pin_title: The quote you already gave is your cheapest lead
pin: Most quotes that go quiet aren't a no. A simple 3-message follow-up (day 2, day 7, day 14) with the exact words to send, for heating and air, plumbing and electrical shops.
long:
The cheapest job you'll book this month is already sitting in your sent folder.

Most homeowners who go quiet on a quote haven't said no. They got busy. The number surprised them. They meant to call you back and the week got away from them. Meanwhile you already paid for that lead: the drive out, the look, the hour writing it up.

Here's a simple rhythm that brings a lot of them back:

1. Day 2: "Hi Karen, just making sure the quote came through okay. Any questions so far?"
2. Day 7: answer the thing they're most likely stuck on. Usually price, timing or "do I really need the whole thing?" Offer a repair-first option or a payment plan if you have one.
3. Day 14: "Should I keep this open for you, or close it out for now?"

That last one gets more replies than you'd think. People like an easy way to answer, even if the answer is "not yet." And "not yet" is a date you can follow up on.

The common mistake: one follow-up, then nothing. Or a "just checking in" with no reason to reply. Every message should make it easy to say one word back.

Put the three dates on the calendar the day the quote goes out, and it stops depending on memory.

How many times does your shop follow up on a quote right now? Zero, one, two, three? Just drop the number.

headline: Ask for the review while you're still in the driveway
points: Text the link before you leave
x:
Ask for the review before you leave the driveway.

"If you were happy with today, mind leaving a quick review? I'll text you the link now."

Then send it right then. Ask everyone the same way. Never offer anything for it.

When does your shop ask now?
pin_title: Ask for the review while you're still in the driveway
pin: When to ask for a Google review (before you leave the driveway), the exact words to say, and the Google rule every shop needs to follow.
long:
The best time to ask for a Google review is while the customer is still standing there, happy the problem is fixed.

Here's why it works: right after the job, the relief is real and fresh. By tomorrow they're back to their busy life, and your request is one more thing on the pile. Most people mean to leave a review. They just never get to it.

How to do it:

1. Before you pull out of the driveway, ask in plain words: "If you were happy with today, would you mind leaving us a quick review? I'll text you the link right now."
2. Actually send the link right then, while you're standing there. One tap for them.
3. Make the link go straight to the review box (Google gives you a short review link in your profile).
4. Ask every customer the same way.

That last one matters. Google's rules say you can't pick only the happy-looking customers, and you can't offer anything in return, like a discount or a gift card. You don't need to. Asking at the right moment is enough.

Example text: "Thanks again, Karen. Here's that link if you have a minute: [link]. It really helps a small shop like ours."

The common mistake: "We'll send you a survey later." Later rarely happens, and a survey isn't a review anyway.

When does your shop ask for reviews right now: on the spot, by text later, by email, or not really at all?

headline: A missed call is a missed job
points: Set it up once, works every day
x:
Most callers who hit voicemail don't leave a message. They call the next shop.

If you can't pick up, text back within 5 minutes:

"Sorry we missed you. This is Mike at Smith Heating. What's going on?"

How fast does your shop call back?
pin_title: A missed call is a missed job
pin: Why missed calls cost home service shops jobs, and the simple text-back message that saves the lead when you can't pick up.
long:
Most people who call a home service company and hit voicemail don't leave a message. They hang up and call the next shop on Google.

Think about why they're calling. Water on the floor. No heat. A breaker that keeps tripping. They want a person, and they want one now. Voicemail feels like "nobody's coming."

If you can't pick up (you're under a sink or in an attic, I get it), the next best thing is a fast text back:

1. Turn on missed-call text back. A lot of business phone apps and phone systems have it built in.
2. Keep the message short and human, with a real name.
3. Ask one simple question so they reply instead of calling the next shop.
4. Then call back as soon as you're out of the crawlspace.

Example: "Sorry we missed your call. This is Mike at Smith Heating. What's going on? I can text a time we can get out there."

That one message turns a hang-up into a conversation.

The common mistake: a long voicemail greeting that lists your hours, your website and your license number. By the time it's done, they've already dialed someone else.

Set it up once and it works every day, including the ones where you're slammed.

How fast does your shop call back a missed call right now? 5 minutes, an hour, end of day? Drop your number.
